steps.text: Part 2 of 4: Forks: how to see them, set them up and stop them. This part covers . Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**A seeing routine.** Search in a fixed order. The Steps method is reported to teach a search routine for each tactic [S, secondary description; manuals not seen]:
1. List enemy pieces that are loose or worth more than yours.
2. Find one square that touches two of them.
3. Can your piece reach it, ideally with check?
4. Run the four answers.
[H] I suspect starting from targets beats starting from your own checks. Test both orders later.

steps.caption: Board A. capture the forker. The knight jump looks like a fork of the king and the queen. Which of the four answers does Black have? Predict, then step through.

line.say: The knight checks the king and attacks the queen on d7.
The pawn on g7 simply takes the knight. A cheap piece answers an expensive threat. This board showed the answer: capture the forker.

claims.statement: The knight attacks the queen on d7.
The pawn on g7 attacks the knight on f6.
Along the engine line the jump loses material.

steps.caption: Board B. check first. The knight jump attacks the queen and the rook. Which of the four answers does Black have? Predict, then step through.

line.say: The knight attacks the queen on a6 and the rook on d7.
The queen escapes with check along the long diagonal.
The king must answer the check.
Now the queen takes the knight. The check bought the tempo. This board showed the answer: check first.

claims.statement: The knight attacks the queen on a6.
The knight attacks the rook on d7.
After the queen move, the queen attacks the king on g2.
Along the engine line the jump loses material.

steps.caption: Board C. defend both. Here the two targets already guard each other. Which of the four answers does Black have? Predict, then step through.

line.say: The knight attacks both bishops, which guard each other along the diagonal.
Black can even ignore the fork.
The knight takes one bishop.
The other bishop takes the knight. A trade, nothing won. This board showed the answer: defend both.

claims.statement: The knight attacks the bishop on c3.
The knight attacks the bishop on f6.
A black piece guards the bishop on c3.
Along the engine line the jump nets no material.

steps.caption: Board D. move one piece and defend the other. Which of the four answers does Black have? Predict, then step through.

line.say: The knight attacks the queen on b7 and the bishop on a4.
The queen moves and now guards the bishop, and eyes the knight too.
The knight takes the bishop.
The queen takes the knight back. Another even trade. This board showed the answer: move one and defend the other.

claims.statement: The knight attacks the queen on b7.
The knight attacks the bishop on a4.
After the queen move, the queen guards the bishop on a4.
After the queen move, the queen attacks the knight on c5.
Along the engine line the jump nets no material.

steps.text: **A fork usually wins when none of the four answers works:** capture the forker, check first, defend both, or move one and defend the other. [I] These four cover the usual replies, not every reply: a bigger counter-threat, such as a mate threat, is a fifth thing to look for. If you find one, write it down; it is a new answer.

**Is the guard real?** Edward Lasker warned that a defender can be an illusion: it may be capturable by a cheaper piece, pulled away or pinned [V-sheet]. The same goes for the pieces a fork attacks. Before you rely on a fork, ask who can capture the forker and whether the target is worth more than your piece. Count what can arrive, not only what is there.

steps.title: Is the target worth taking?
steps.prompt: Both knight jumps check the king and attack a piece on a6. Look at both boards, name the one thing that differs, and predict which jump wins material.

steps.title: Can the opponent check first?
steps.prompt: Both knight jumps attack a rook and a bishop. Look at both boards, name the one thing that differs, and predict which jump wins material.

steps.title: Is the landing square guarded?
steps.prompt: Both knight jumps check the king and attack the rook. Look at both boards, name the one thing that differs, and predict which jump wins material.

steps.text: **Setting one up.** Often the fork is not on the board yet. Forcing moves, such as a check, a capture or a threat, leave the opponent no time to choose, so they can drag a king, a queen or a rook onto the forking lines. Ask of each forcing move: where must the reply land, and does that square touch a fork?

steps.caption: A check can drag the king to the fork square. Black to move.

line.say: The rook checks, and the white king has to go somewhere.
The king steps to g2, a square the black knight can fork from.
The knight checks the king and attacks the rook on c2.
The king moves again.
The knight takes the rook.

claims.statement: The knight attacks the king on g2.
The knight attacks the rook on c2.
Along the engine line the check wins material.

steps.caption: A capture can drag a piece to the fork square. White to move.

line.say: The queens trade: a capture forces a recapture.
The rook recaptures and lands on f4.
The knight checks the king on g7 and attacks the rook on f4.
The king steps aside.
The knight takes the rook.

claims.statement: The knight attacks the king on g7.
The knight attacks the rook on f4.
Along the engine line the queen trade wins material.

steps.caption: A quiet threat can set it up. White to move.

line.say: The knight attacks the rook on d8 and the pawn on a7.
The rook moves.
The knight jumps again, checking the king and attacking the bishop on f5.
The king steps aside.
The knight takes the bishop.

claims.statement: The knight attacks the rook on d8.
The knight attacks the king on g8.
The knight attacks the bishop on f5.
Along the engine line the knight move wins material.
